title: Index an off-balance rotary table 90 degrees and lock it with a pin
instruction: Turn the rotary table 90 degrees clockwise by its peg and lock it there: drop the pin through the plate's hole into the base hole at the white mark.
context: Machinists index rotary tables and lock them with a pin before cutting. With a heavy off-centre fixture on a tilted table, the plate swings back the moment it is let go, so one hand holds it on station while the other drops the locking pin.
setup: Station table; distances from the arm bases' line are forward, and left or right from the point midway between the arms. A fixed square steel base (25 x 25 x 1.2 cm) on four steel legs, centred 22 cm forward at the midpoint, tilted 7 degrees down toward the left, its top 4.5 cm above the table at the centre. A steel post 16 mm across and 2.4 cm tall stands at the base's centre. Three steel ball transfers on a 5 cm radius stand 4 mm proud of the base, giving a friction of 0.01. The base has two square index holes 16 mm wide, each 8 cm from the post: the 90-degree hole straight to the left of the post, and the 45-degree hole halfway between left and toward the arms. A small white mark on the table beside the base's left edge, in line with the post, marks the 90-degree hole, and a yellow mark 10.5 cm nearer the arms marks the other. A one-piece HDPE plastic rotary plate (0.8 kg in all) rests on the ball transfers around the post, through a square hole 18 mm wide: a 20 x 20 x 1 cm plate with a 10 x 6 x 7 cm red fixture block on its top, centred 7 cm to the left of the post at home, and a 2 x 2 x 4 cm yellow peg, 8 cm forward of the post at home. The plate has one square hole 20 mm wide, 8 cm toward the arms from the post at home, so it lies over the 90-degree hole when the plate has turned 90 degrees clockwise seen from above. At home, the fixture rests at the low side. A hollow steel pin (10 mm shaft with a rounded nose, 6 cm long, under a 22 mm head 6 mm thick, 30 g) stands in a square steel socket (11 mm hole, 3 cm deep, walls 1 cm thick) centred 17 cm forward and 24 cm left of the midpoint.
scoring: The plate's angle is how far it has turned clockwise from home about the post. The pin is in a hole when it is within 12 degrees of upright, its axis within 5 mm of the hole's centre at the base's top, and its foot below the base's top. 1.0 if the pin is in the 90-degree hole, the plate is within 8 degrees of 90, and for 1 second the plate is still and the pin isn't moving. 0.5 if the plate ends within 8 degrees of 90 without the pin in that hole. 0.25 if the pin is in the 45-degree hole with the plate within 8 degrees of 45. 0 otherwise. In a real trial, a protractor printed on the base gives the angle, and a photo from above shows which hole holds the pin.
reset_notes: Lift the pin out, let the plate swing back to home, and stand the pin in its socket; nothing is consumed.
fidelity: All parts are rigid. The plate rides on three low-friction balls around a plain post, and its off-centre weight comes from one piece of uniform density, in place of a real table's bearing and a separate heavy fixture. The holes are square where a real index plate's are round, and the wide plate hole acts as a lead-in, leaving a pinned plate about 6 degrees off 90. Nothing is deformable.
